{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Base directory for this skill: /logs/agent/sessions/skills/marker\n\n# Marker PDF-to-Markdown Converter\n\nConvert PDFs to Markdown while preserving LaTeX formulas and document structure. Uses the `marker_single` CLI from the marker-pdf package.\n\n## Dependencies\n- `marker_single` on PATH (`pip install marker-pdf` if missing)\n- Python 3.10+ (available in the task image)\n\n## Quick Start\n\n```python\nfrom scripts.marker_to_markdown import pdf_to_markdown\n\nmarkdown_text = pdf_to_markdown(\"paper.pdf\")\nprint(markdown_text)\n```\n\n## Python API\n\n- `pdf_to_markdown(pdf_path, *, timeout=600, cleanup=True) -> str`\n  - Runs `marker_single --output_format markdown --disable_image_extraction`\n  - `cleanup=True`: use a temp directory and delete after reading the Markdown\n  - `cleanup=False`: keep outputs in `<pdf_stem>_marker/` next to the PDF\n  - Exceptions: `FileNotFoundError` if the PDF is missing, `RuntimeError` for marker failures, `TimeoutError` if it exceeds the timeout\n- Tips: bump `timeout` for large PDFs; set `cleanup=False` to inspect intermediate files\n\n## Command-Line Usage\n\n```bash\n# Basic conversion (prints markdown to stdout)\npython scripts/marker_to_markdown.py paper.pdf\n\n# Keep temporary files\npython scripts/marker_to_markdown.py paper.pdf --keep-temp\n\n# Custom timeout\npython scripts/marker_to_markdown.py paper.pdf --timeout 600\n```\n\n## Output Locations\n- `cleanup=True`: outputs stored in a temporary directory and removed automatically\n- `cleanup=False`: outputs saved to `<pdf_stem>_marker/`; markdown lives at `<pdf_stem>_marker/<pdf_stem>/<pdf_stem>.md` when present (otherwise the first `.md` file is used)\n\n## Troubleshooting\n- `marker_single` not found: install `marker-pdf` or ensure the CLI is on PATH\n- No Markdown output: re-run with `--keep-temp`/`cleanup=False` and check `stdout`/`stderr` saved in the output folder\n\n\nARGUMENTS: latex_paper.pdf"}]},"parent_tool_use_id":null,"session_id":"f604c07f-1955-409b-9e74-bef8d5cddc7a","uuid":"92f283f7-d978-4bf5-ad5b-3ef94ae4d6de","isSynthetic":true}

{"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_vrtx_014DQLmq3dimzrWBCspjjRdh","type":"tool_result","content":"Number of pages: 3\n==================================================\n\n--- Page 1 ---\nTemporally multiplexed ion-photon quantum interface via fast ion-chain transport\nBingran You,1, 2 Qiming Wu,1, 2, ∗David Miron,1, 2 Wenjun Ke,1\nInder Monga,2 Erhan Saglamyurek,1, 2 and Hartmut Haeffner1, 2, †\n1Department of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94270, USA\n2Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA\n(Dated: January 12, 2026)\nHigh-rate remote entanglement between photon and matter-based qubits is essential for dis-\ntributed quantum information processing. A key technique to increase the modest entangling rates\nof existing long-distance quantum networking approaches is multiplexing. Here, we demonstrate\na temporally multiplexed ion-photon interface via rapid transport of a chain of nine calcium ions\nacross 74 µm within 86 µs. The non-classical nature of the multiplexed photons is verified by mea-\nsuring the second-order correlation function with an average value of g(2)(0) = 0.060(13), indicating\nnegligible crosstalk between the multiplexed modes.\nIn addition, we characterize the motional\ndegree-of-freedom of the ion crystal after transport and find that it is coherently excited to as much\nas ¯nα ≈110 for the center-of-mass mode. Our proof-of-principle implementation paves the way\nfor large-scale quantum networking with trapped ions, but highlights some challenges that must be\novercome.\nRemote entanglement across distant quantum nodes [?\n? ] may be used for long-distance quantum key distribu-\ntion [? ? ], modular quantum computer architectures [?\n? ], as well as quantum enhanced metrology and sens-\ning [? ? ? ]. Light-matter quantum interfaces are a fun-\ndamental building block for such applications, and allow\nfor distributed entanglement between stationary matter\nqubits by using \"flying\" photons.\nFor practical purposes, these quantum interfaces need\nto be capable of establishing remote entanglement at\nhigh rates across a large-scale network of quantum nodes.\nHowever, in widely adopted probabilistic schemes based\non heralded photon detection [? ? ? ], it is infeasible to\ndistribute entanglement at useful rates over a few kilo-\nmeters, as the attempt rate is limited by the round-trip\ntravel-time of photons in a single mode. For example, for\na communication distance of 10 km, photon-travel time\nwill be around 100 µs, meaning that the attempt can-\nnot be higher than 10 kHz. In this scenario, even with\nuse of a state-of-the-art photon-matter interface that can\nyield close to unity photon extraction efficiency [? ], the\nmatter-photon entanglement rate beyond tens of kilome-\nters would be limited to sub 10 s−1 with total loss around\n15 dB after considering the collective probability of gener-\nating and detecting telecom photons at each node, along\nwith the optical fiber loss [? ? ].\nA key solution to this challenge is multiplexing: to\ncombine multiple signals into a single channel and there-\nfore increase the attempt rate [? ? ]. Multiplexing has\nbecome a mature technology for ensemble-based quan-\ntum interfa\n...\n\n--- Page 2 ---\n2\nThe schematics of the experimental procedures is illus-\ntrated in Fig. ??(a). Our experiment is conducted using\nan RF Paul trap, composed of four RF blades for generat-\ning radial pseudopotential and two DC endcap electrodes\nfor providing an axial harmonic confinement. We typi-\ncally trap a string of nine 40Ca+ ions in a linear configu-\nration with the COM mode frequency of ωx,z/(2π) = ×\n{1.15, 0.179} MHz and Lamb-Dicke (LD) parameters of\nthe axial modes, ranging between 0.09 and 0.23 on the\n42S1/2 ↔32D5/2 transition. Two global laser beams at\n397 nm and 866 nm (not shown in the figure) evenly il-\nluminate the entire ion chain for Doppler cooling and\noptical pumping, and a tightly focused addressing beam\nat 866 nm allows for resonant excitation to extract the\n397 nm single photons from individual ions. The gener-\nated single photons are collected by an objective with\na numerical aperture of NA = 0.3 (collection efficiency\nPc ≈2.5%) and directed to a 50/50 beam splitter (BS).\nAt the exit port of BS, photons are detected by two pho-\ntomultiplier tube (PMT)-based single-photon detectors\n(SPD), and their arrival times are recorded with a time-\ntagger for subsequent analysis.\nWe generate on-demand single-photons based on a\nbackground-free scheme, as illustrated in Fig. ??(b) [?\n].\nIn this process, we first Doppler cool (detuning\n∆= −Γ/2) the ion chain for 200 µs, with the first 100 µs\nassisted by another beam −500 MHz detuned from the\n42S1/2 ↔42P1/2 transition (not shown) to mitigate col-\nlision induced ion chain melting in the Paul trap [? ].\nThen we begin the photon generation sequences with\noptical pumping to the 32D3/2 state for 3 µs, followed\nby transport of the chain to position each ion in the\ntight focus of the 866 nm addressing beam resonant with\n32D3/2 ↔42P1/2 transition to generate 397 nm single\nphotons (see Fig. ??(c)).\nIn the ion-chain transport process, the endcap volt-\nages are controlled by an arbitrary waveform generator\n(AWG) amplified by a custom-made, low-noise amplifier\ncircuit with a gain of ten through low-pass filters and\na vacuum feedthrough. The low-pass filters have cutoff\nfrequencies of 1.9 MHz to allow fast transport of the ion\nchain close to the speed of the COM mode frequency.\nThe programmed and the measured waveform show a\nnegligible latency effect from the filters (Fig. ??(a)). The\nforward shuttling function has eight steps, during each of\nwhich a different ion is placed in the focus of the address-\ning beam for 1.7 µs with the beam turned on simultane-\nously. After completing this sequence, we move the entire\nion chain back to the original position in 35 µs using the\nsame function form in one step.\nThe voltage ramping\nfunction on the two endcaps V1,2(t) is in the form of a\nsigmoid-like polynomial function such that the first and\nsecond order derivative at the beginning and the end of\nthe transport vanish [? ].\nd2xi\ndt2 = −ω2\n0xi + kq2\nm\nN\nX\nj=1\nj̸=i\n1\n(xi −xj)2 · sgn (xi −xj) (1)\nwhere ∆V is the voltage difference b\n...\n\n--- Page 3 ---\n3\nthe ions’ motional states.\nWe further explore the sys-\ntem performance by measuring the motional heating from\nthe ion transport.\nTo do this, we first perform side-\nband cooling for all axial modes sequentially using the\nmethod similar to that in [? ] and prepare the ion in\nthe state |↓⟩= |42S1/2, mJ = −1/2⟩. We compare the\n|↓⟩↔|↑⟩= |32D5/2, mJ = −1/2⟩carrier transition be-\nfore and after transport with a global 729 nm beam along\nthe axial direction to determine how the transport af-\nfects the ion-motion (Fig. ??). The carrier Rabi flopping\nis motional state sensitive, and the Hamiltonian has the\nform of [? ? ]\nHi,M = (ℏ/2)Ω(i)σ(i)\nx\nM\nY\nm=1\nexp\n\u0002\niηi,m\n\u0002\nam + a†\nm\n\u0001\u0003\n,\n(3)\nwhere Ω(i) is the Rabi frequency of the ith ion, am and a†\nm\nare the creation and annihilation operators on the mth\nmode, and ηi,m is the LD parameter of the ith ion and the\nmth mode. Considering the computational difficulty of\nincluding all motional modes in the simulation, we only\nconsider the COM mode which we expect to be excited\nmost because the electric fields, both from the transport\nand surface noise, are correlated over the whole ion string\n(see Supplemental [? ]). Therefore, the average carrier\nRabi flopping can be simplified to\nPe(t) =\n1\n2N\n\"\n1 −\n∞\nX\nn=0\nN\nX\ni=0\nPn cos\n\u0010\nΩ(i)\nn t\n\u0011#\n,\n(4)\nwhere Pn is the occupation on the nth number state and\nencodes a convolution between a thermal and a coher-\nent phonon distribution [? ]. Ω(i)\nn\nis the Rabi frequency\nof the ith ion on the nth number state [?\n].\nTo ver-\nify the effectiveness of our approximation, we probe the\nsideband-cooled motional spectrum of the nine-ion chain\nbefore the tranport and verify that only the COM mode\nis not cooled to near the ground state [? ], for which\nwe find a cooling limit of ¯nth = 4.0 ± 3.0.\nWe also\nmeasure the electric-field noise induced heating and find\na heating rate of 20 quanta / ms.(Fig. ??(a)), indicating\nthat the remaining thermal population is likely limited\nby the COM mode heating which scales as ion number\nN [? ]. Fig. ??(b) shows the carrier Rabi flopping after\nion transport twice as slow as in Fig. ??(a). From nu-\nmerical simulations (blue line), we find that the data can\nbe explained well by a coherent state ¯nα = |α|2 ≈50 on\nthe COM mode after the transport. Similarly, we per-\nform the full-speed tranport and the carrier Rabi flop-\nping matches with COM coherent state with ¯nα ≈110\n(Fig. ??(c)). As shown in the Rabi flopping plots, there\nis mismatch between the experimental data and numeri-\ncal simulation at full speed, which could be due to ther-\nmal and coherent occupation of other modes and will\nrequire additional investigation. For example, one can\nuse an individual 729 nm addressing beam to probe the\nblue sideband transition of different modes [? ]. The op-\ntimal fast transport of a long ion chain remains an open\nquestion and is beyond the scope of this work. {"type":"user","message":{"role":"user","content":[{"tool_use_id":"toolu_vrtx_0172tXJ9mpRcLagVGcpETE9A","type":"tool_result","content":"============================================================\nPAGE 1\n============================================================\nTemporally multiplexed ion-photon quantum interface via fast ion-chain transport\nBingran You,1, 2 Qiming Wu,1, 2, ∗David Miron,1, 2 Wenjun Ke,1\nInder Monga,2 Erhan Saglamyurek,1, 2 and Hartmut Haeffner1, 2, †\n1Department of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94270, USA\n2Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA\n(Dated: January 12, 2026)\nHigh-rate remote entanglement between photon and matter-based qubits is essential for dis-\ntributed quantum information processing. A key technique to increase the modest entangling rates\nof existing long-distance quantum networking approaches is multiplexing. Here, we demonstrate\na temporally multiplexed ion-photon interface via rapid transport of a chain of nine calcium ions\nacross 74 µm within 86 µs. The non-classical nature of the multiplexed photons is verified by mea-\nsuring the second-order correlation function with an average value of g(2)(0) = 0.060(13), indicating\nnegligible crosstalk between the multiplexed modes.\nIn addition, we characterize the motional\ndegree-of-freedom of the ion crystal after transport and find that it is coherently excited to as much\nas ¯nα ≈110 for the center-of-mass mode. Our proof-of-principle implementation paves the way\nfor large-scale quantum networking with trapped ions, but highlights some challenges that must be\novercome.\nRemote entanglement across distant quantum nodes [?\n? ] may be used for long-distance quantum key distribu-\ntion [? ? ], modular quantum computer architectures [?\n? ], as well as quantum enhanced metrology and sens-\ning [? ? ? ]. Light-matter quantum interfaces are a fun-\ndamental building block for such applications, and allow\nfor distributed entanglement between stationary matter\nqubits by using \"flying\" photons.\nFor practical purposes, these quantum interfaces need\nto be capable of establishing remote entanglement at\nhigh rates across a large-scale network of quantum nodes.\nHowever, in widely adopted probabilistic schemes based\non heralded photon detection [? ? ? ], it is infeasible to\ndistribute entanglement at useful rates over a few kilo-\nmeters, as the attempt rate is limited by the round-trip\ntravel-time of photons in a single mode. For example, for\na communication distance of 10 km, photon-travel time\nwill be around 100 µs, meaning that the attempt can-\nnot be higher than 10 kHz. In this scenario, even with\nuse of a state-of-the-art photon-matter interface that can\nyield close to unity photon extraction efficiency [? ], the\nmatter-photon entanglement rate beyond tens of kilome-\nters would be limited to sub 10 s−1 with total loss around\n15 dB after considering the collective probability of gener-\nating and detecting telecom photons at each node, along\nwith the optical fiber loss [? ? ].\nA key solution to this challenge is multiplexing: to\ncombine multiple signals into a single channel and there-\nfore increase the attempt rate [? ? ]. Multiplexing has\nbecome a mature technology for ensemble-based quan-\ntum interfaces, both in atomic gases and rare-earth ion\ndoped solid-state systems [? ? ? ? ]. However, large-\nscale local quantum information processing is technically\nchallenging in these platforms [? ].\nIn contrast, single emitters, including trapped ions and\nneutral atoms, offer excellent local quantum information\nprocessing capability beside their natural interface with\nlight at convenient wavelengths for quantum frequency\nconversion (QFC) [?\n?\n], and the possibility of long-\nlived storage of entanglement [? ? ]. On the other hand,\nimplementing a multiplexed light-matter interface with\nthese systems is technically challenging. Towards over-\ncoming this problem, a few multiplexing schemes have\nalready been proposed for ion and atom-based quantum\nprocessors [? ? ? ? ]. The only reported experimental\nwork, we are aware of, is the demonstration of multi-\nplexing using a static three-ion chain [? ]. In view of the\nrecent advances of the quantum CCD architecture [? ? ?\n], a complementary approach to multiplexing is the pro-\ncess of ion-transport through a specific spatial location\nwith maximized photon coupling efficiency.\nIn this work, we demonstrate a temporal multiplexing\nscheme based on the transport of an ion-chain for improv-\ning the rate of ion-photon entanglement over long dis-\ntances. In our experiments, we generate on-demand sin-\ngle photons by shuttling a nine-ion chain across the focus\nof a single-ion addressing beam. This scheme is expected\nto lead to a nearly nine-fold increase in attempt rate of\nthe entanglement generation for quantum repeater nodes\nseparated by >100 km. We verify the single-photon na-\nture of the photon trains by measuring a second-order\ntime correlation of g(2)(0) = 0.060(13) without back-\nground subtraction. Furthermore, we address the prob-\nlem of motional excitation during the transport, which\nis detrimental to local entangling operations [? ] and\nin the case of using a cavity for stimulating the photons\nwould lead to uncertainly in the coupling strength. [?\n]. Using a shuttling function designed to mitigate mo-\ntional excitation, we find coherent excitation of ¯nα ∼50\non the center-of-mass (COM) mode during one round of\nion chain transport.\nThese results show that the pro-\nposed multiplexing scheme can be scaled up to higher\nrates provided that more optimal transport methods are\napplied.\n\n\n============================================================\nPAGE 2\n============================================================\n2\nThe schematics of the experimental procedures is illus-\ntrated in Fig. ??(a). Our experiment is conducted using\nan RF Paul trap, composed of four RF blades for generat-\ning radial pseudopotential and two DC endcap electrodes\nfor providing an axial harmonic confinement. We typi-\ncally trap a string of nine 40Ca+ ions in a linear configu-\nration with the COM mode frequency of ωx,z/(2π) = ×\n{1.15, 0.179} MHz and Lamb-Dicke (LD) parameters of\nthe axial modes, ranging between 0.09 and 0.23 on the\n42S1/2 ↔32D5/2 transition. Two global laser beams at\n397 nm and 866 nm (not shown in the figure) evenly il-\nluminate the entire ion chain for Doppler cooling and\noptical pumping, and a tightly focused addressing beam\nat 866 nm allows for resonant excitation to extract the\n397 nm single photons from individual ions. The gener-\nated single photons are collected by an objective with\na numerical aperture of NA = 0.3 (collection efficiency\nPc ≈2.5%) and directed to a 50/50 beam splitter (BS).\nAt the exit port of BS, photons are detected by two pho-\ntomultiplier tube (PMT)-based single-photon detectors\n(SPD), and their arrival times are recorded with a time-\ntagger for subsequent analysis.\nWe generate on-demand single-photons based on a\nbackground-free scheme, as illustrated in Fig. ??(b) [?\n].\nIn this process, we first Doppler cool (detuning\n∆= −Γ/2) the ion chain for 200 µs, with the first 100 µs\nassisted by another beam −500 MHz detuned from the\n42S1/2 ↔42P1/2 transition (not shown) to mitigate col-\nlision induced ion chain melting in the Paul trap [? ].\nThen we begin the photon generation sequences with\noptical pumping to the 32D3/2 state for 3 µs, followed\nby transport of the chain to position each ion in the\ntight focus of the 866 nm addressing beam resonant with\n32D3/2 ↔42P1/2 transition to generate 397 nm single\nphotons (see Fig. ??(c)).\nIn the ion-chain transport process, the endcap volt-\nages are controlled by an arbitrary waveform generator\n(AWG) amplified by a custom-made, low-noise amplifier\ncircuit with a gain of ten through low-pass filters and\na vacuum feedthrough. The low-pass filters have cutoff\nfrequencies of 1.9 MHz to allow fast transport of the ion\nchain close to the speed of the COM mode frequency.\nThe programmed and the measured waveform show a\nnegligible latency effect from the filters (Fig. ??(a)). The\nforward shuttling function has eight steps, during each of\nwhich a different ion is placed in the focus of the address-\ning beam for 1.7 µs with the beam turned on simultane-\nously. After completing this sequence, we move the entire\nion chain back to the original position in 35 µs using the\nsame function form in one step.\nThe voltage ramping\nfunction on the two endcaps V1,2(t) is in the form of a\nsigmoid-like polynomial function such that the first and\nsecond order derivative at the beginning and the end of\nthe transport vanish [? ].\nd2xi\ndt2 = −ω2\n0xi + kq2\nm\nN\nX\nj=1\nj̸=i\n1\n(xi −xj)2 · sgn (xi −xj) (1)\nwhere ∆V is the voltage difference between the be-\nginning and the end of a step, t is the time after the\nend of the previous step, and T = 9.1 µs is the total\ntime of each transport. The details of voltage optimiza-\ntion and numerical simulation of motional heating can\nbe found in [? ]. We reconstruct the temporal profile of\n397 nm photons during transport using the recorded ar-\nrival times of photons on the PMTs. Fig ??(b) shows the\nemission from individual ions (modes). Data is accumu-\nlated for 40 min, during which around 1.56×106 attempts\nwere made to the whole string, corresponding to attempt\nrate 39.0 kHz, an average photon extraction efficiency of\n0.21 % and single photons count rate of around 71 cps.\nNext, we perform a two-photon correlation experiment\nto test the non-classical characteristics of our multiplexed\nphoton source [? ]. The probability of two-photon corre-\nlation when detecting a correlation event on two detectors\nat different times is given by\nρc(τ) = ρ1(τ)ρ2(τ + δT),\n(2)\nwhere ρ1(τ) and ρ2(τ + δT) are the probability of de-\ntecting a photon at t = τ and τ + δT on detector 1 and\n2. Fig. ??(a) shows the normalized correlation counts as\na function of the delay mode window. We choose a co-\nincidence window of 300 ns in each mode and measure\n8 coincident counts at zero delay in 4.8 hours, corre-\nsponding to g(2)(0) = 0.060(13). The residual correla-\ntion can be explained by excitation of neighboring ions,\ni.e., crosstalk of the addressing beam, which is sepa-\nrately characterized to be 0.99 % using fluorescence of\nthe nine-ion chain on the camera, corresponding to ex-\npected average g(2)\nexp(0) = 0.049(8) (see Supplemental [?\n]). To further verify this hypothesis, we repeat the mea-\nsurement with a single ion (Fig. ??(c)) and compare\nit to addressing only the fifth ion in a static nine-ion\nchain (Fig. ??(b)). The two experiments yield g(2)(0) =\n0.010(6) and g(2)(0) = 0.062(17) with 6.0 and 4.8 hours\nof data accumulation, respectively. While the single ion\ng2 is limited by the detector dark counts and ambient\nlight, the measurement of the static 9-ion chain g2 is\nlimited by the crosstalk of the addressing beam.\nThe\nresults indicate the major source of residual correlation\nis addressing crosstalk [? ]. This can be mitigated by\ncoupling the single photons into a single-mode fiber or\nimproving the optical quality of the excitation beam.\nAfter characterizing the single-photon nature of the\ntransport-multiplexing scheme, we characterize the mo-\ntion of the ions introduced by shuttling. This is impor-\ntant as the quality of subsequent quantum operations\non the ions or ion-photon entanglement will depend on\n\n\n============================================================\nPAGE 3\n============================================================\n3\nthe ions’ motional states.\nWe further explore the sys-\ntem performance by measuring the motional heating from\nthe ion transport.\nTo do this, we first perform side-\nband cooling for all axial modes sequentially using the\nmethod similar to that in [? ] and prepare the ion in\nthe state |↓⟩= |42S1/2, mJ = −1/2⟩. We compare the\n|↓⟩↔|↑⟩= |32D5/2, mJ = −1/2⟩carrier transition be-\nfore and after transport with a global 729 nm beam along\nthe axial direction to determine how the transport af-\nfects the ion-motion (Fig. ??). The carrier Rabi flopping\nis motional state sensitive, and the Hamiltonian has the\nform of [? ? ]\nHi,M = (ℏ/2)Ω(i)σ(i)\nx\nM\nY\nm=1\nexp\n\u0002\niηi,m\n\u0002\nam + a†\nm\n\u0001\u0003\n,\n(3)\nwhere Ω(i) is the Rabi frequency of the ith ion, am and a†\nm\nare the creation and annihilation operators on the mth\nmode, and ηi,m is the LD parameter of the ith ion and the\nmth mode. Considering the computational difficulty of\nincluding all motional modes in the simulation, we only\nconsider the COM mode which we expect to be excited\nmost because the electric fields, both from the transport\nand surface noise, are correlated over the whole ion string\n(see Supplemental [? ]). Therefore, the average carrier\nRabi flopping can be simplified to\nPe(t) =\n1\n2N\n\"\n1 −\n∞\nX\nn=0\nN\nX\ni=0\nPn cos\n\u0010\nΩ(i)\nn t\n\u0011#\n,\n(4)\nwhere Pn is the occupation on the nth number state and\nencodes a convolution between a thermal and a coher-\nent phonon distribution [? ]. Ω(i)\nn\nis the Rabi frequency\nof the ith ion on the nth number state [?\n].\nTo ver-\nify the effectiveness of our approximation, we probe the\nsideband-cooled motional spectrum of the nine-ion chain\nbefore the tranport and verify that only the COM mode\nis not cooled to near the ground state [? ], for which\nwe find a cooling limit of ¯nth = 4.0 ± 3.0.\nWe also\nmeasure the electric-field noise induced heating and find\na heating rate of 20 quanta / ms.(Fig. ??(a)), indicating\nthat the remaining thermal population is likely limited\nby the COM mode heating which scales as ion number\nN [? ]. Fig. ??(b) shows the carrier Rabi flopping after\nion transport twice as slow as in Fig. ??(a). From nu-\nmerical simulations (blue line), we find that the data can\nbe explained well by a coherent state ¯nα = |α|2 ≈50 on\nthe COM mode after the transport. Similarly, we per-\nform the full-speed tranport and the carrier Rabi flop-\nping matches with COM coherent state with ¯nα ≈110\n(Fig. ??(c)). As shown in the Rabi flopping plots, there\nis mismatch between the experimental data and numeri-\ncal simulation at full speed, which could be due to ther-\nmal and coherent occupation of other modes and will\nrequire additional investigation. For example, one can\nuse an individual 729 nm addressing beam to probe the\nblue sideband transition of different modes [? ]. The op-\ntimal fast transport of a long ion chain remains an open\nquestion and is beyond the scope of this work. However,\nwe note that further optimization can be done by energy\nself-neutral shuttling [? ? ], implementing closed-loop\noptimization of the shuttling function [? ], etc.\nTo summarize, we have presented a multiplexed ion-\nphoton interface by transporting a nine-ion chain with\nsynchronized excitation in sub-hundred µs. The speed\nis restricted by the motional frequency and can be in-\ncreased by an order of magnitude, for instance, using a\n3D-printed ion trap [? ] with radial frequency beyond\n10 MHz. The 397 nm photon can be converted to the\ntelecommunication band via a two-step QFC [? ]. Once\nintegrated with state preparation on 32D3/2 Zeeman sub-\nlevel and photon collection with a single mode fiber, we\nexpect a faster photon extraction rate [? ] and negligi-\nble ion crosstalk while achieving high fidelity ion-photon\nentanglement [? ? ]. Our system can also be combined\nwith a miniature cavity [?\n]\nfor much higher photon\nextraction efficiency without sacrificing the photon gen-\neration rate, while the ion’s positional spread caused by\ncoherent excitation can be mitigated by aligning the cav-\nity along the radial direction or further optimization of\nthe shuttling function. These results stimulate the re-\nsearch of fast shuttling of a chain of tens of ions as a\nunit cell of logical qubit with heralded entanglement [?\n]\nand high-rates entanglement of quantum processors\nacross large distances.\nB.Y and Q.W have contributed equally to this work.\nWe thank Alp Sipahigil, Ben Lanyon, Tracy Northup,\nYou-Wei Hsieh, and Wenji Wu for their helpful discus-\nsion. The residual correla-\ntion can be explained by excitation of neighboring ions,\ni.e., crosstalk of the addressing beam, which is sepa-\nrately characterized to be 0.99 % using fluorescence of\nthe nine-ion chain on the camera, corresponding to ex-\npected average g(2)\nexp(0) = 0.049(8) (see Supplemental [?\n]). To further verify this hypothesis, we repeat the mea-\nsurement with a single ion (Fig. ??(c)) and compare\nit to addressing only the fifth ion in a static nine-ion\nchain (Fig. ??(b)). The two experiments yield g(2)(0) =\n0.010(6) and g(2)(0) = 0.062(17) with 6.0 and 4.8 hours\nof data accumulation, respectively. While the single ion\ng2 is limited by the detector dark counts and ambient\nlight, the measurement of the static 9-ion chain g2 is\nlimited by the crosstalk of the addressing beam.\nThe\nresults indicate the major source of residual correlation\nis addressing crosstalk [? ]. This can be mitigated by\ncoupling the single photons into a single-mode fiber or\nimproving the optical quality of the excitation beam.\nAfter characterizing the single-photon nature of the\ntransport-multiplexing scheme, we characterize the mo-\ntion of the ions introduced by shuttling. This is impor-\ntant as the quality of subsequent quantum operations\non the ions or ion-photon entanglement will depend on\n\n\n============================================================\nPAGE 3\n============================================================\n3\nthe ions’ motional states.\nWe further explore the sys-\ntem performance by measuring the motional heating from\nthe ion transport.\nTo do this, we first perform side-\nband cooling for all axial modes sequentially using the\nmethod similar to that in [? ] and prepare the ion in\nthe state |↓⟩= |42S1/2, mJ = −1/2⟩. We compare the\n|↓⟩↔|↑⟩= |32D5/2, mJ = −1/2⟩carrier transition be-\nfore and after transport with a global 729 nm beam along\nthe axial direction to determine how the transport af-\nfects the ion-motion (Fig. ??). The carrier Rabi flopping\nis motional state sensitive, and the Hamiltonian has the\nform of [? ? ]\nHi,M = (ℏ/2)Ω(i)σ(i)\nx\nM\nY\nm=1\nexp\n\u0002\niηi,m\n\u0002\nam + a†\nm\n\u0001\u0003\n,\n(3)\nwhere Ω(i) is the Rabi frequency of the ith ion, am and a†\nm\nare the creation and annihilation operators on the mth\nmode, and ηi,m is the LD parameter of the ith ion and the\nmth mode. Considering the computational difficulty of\nincluding all motional modes in the simulation, we only\nconsider the COM mode which we expect to be excited\nmost because the electric fields, both from the transport\nand surface noise, are correlated over the whole ion string\n(see Supplemental [? ]). Therefore, the average carrier\nRabi flopping can be simplified to\nPe(t) =\n1\n2N\n\"\n1 −\n∞\nX\nn=0\nN\nX\ni=0\nPn cos\n\u0010\nΩ(i)\nn t\n\u0011#\n,\n(4)\nwhere Pn is the occupation on the nth number state and\nencodes a convolution between a thermal and a coher-\nent phonon distribution [? ]. Ω(i)\nn\nis the Rabi frequency\nof the ith ion on the nth number state [?\n].\nTo ver-\nify the effectiveness of our approximation, we probe the\nsideband-cooled motional spectrum of the nine-ion chain\nbefore the tranport and verify that only the COM mode\nis not cooled to near the ground state [? ], for which\nwe find a cooling limit of ¯nth = 4.0 ± 3.0.\nWe also\nmeasure the electric-field noise induced heating and find\na heating rate of 20 quanta / ms.(Fig. ??(a)), indicating\nthat the remaining thermal population is likely limited\nby the COM mode heating which scales as ion number\nN [? ]. Fig. ??(b) shows the carrier Rabi flopping after\nion transport twice as slow as in Fig. ??(a). From nu-\nmerical simulations (blue line), we find that the data can\nbe explained well by a coherent state ¯nα = |α|2 ≈50 on\nthe COM mode after the transport. Similarly, we per-\nform the full-speed tranport and the carrier Rabi flop-\nping matches with COM coherent state with ¯nα ≈110\n(Fig. ??(c)). As shown in the Rabi flopping plots, there\nis mismatch between the experimental data and numeri-\ncal simulation at full speed, which could be due to ther-\nmal and coherent occupation of other modes and will\nrequire additional investigation. For example, one can\nuse an individual 729 nm addressing beam to probe the\nblue sideband transition of different modes [? ]. The op-\ntimal fast transport of a long ion chain remains an open\nquestion and is beyond the scope of this work. However,\nwe note that further optimization can be done by energy\nself-neutral shuttling [? ? ], implementing closed-loop\noptimization of the shuttling function [? ], etc.\nTo summarize, we have presented a multiplexed ion-\nphoton interface by transporting a nine-ion chain with\nsynchronized excitation in sub-hundred µs. The speed\nis restricted by the motional frequency and can be in-\ncreased by an order of magnitude, for instance, using a\n3D-printed ion trap [? ] with radial frequency beyond\n10 MHz. The 397 nm photon can be converted to the\ntelecommunication band via a two-step QFC [? ]. Once\nintegrated with state preparation on 32D3/2 Zeeman sub-\nlevel and photon collection with a single mode fiber, we\nexpect a faster photon extraction rate [? ] and negligi-\nble ion crosstalk while achieving high fidelity ion-photon\nentanglement [? ? ]. Our system can also be combined\nwith a miniature cavity [?\n]\nfor much higher photon\nextraction efficiency without sacrificing the photon gen-\neration rate, while the ion’s positional spread caused by\ncoherent excitation can be mitigated by aligning the cav-\nity along the radial direction or further optimization of\nthe shuttling function. These results stimulate the re-\nsearch of fast shuttling of a chain of tens of ions as a\nunit cell of logical qubit with heralded entanglement [?\n]\nand high-rates entanglement of quantum processors\nacross large distances.\nB.Y and Q.W have contributed equally to this work.\nWe thank Alp Sipahigil, Ben Lanyon, Tracy Northup,\nYou-Wei Hsieh, and Wenji Wu for their helpful discus-\nsion. Q.W. and H.H. acknowledge funding by the U.S.\nDepartment of Energy, Office of Science, Office of Basic\nEnergy Sciences under Awards No. DE-SC0023277.
